\chapter{Agreeing, Differing, and Saying Why}
\label{ch:bn-agreeing-differing-saying-why}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can agree with somebody and disagree with them, turn a second clause against the first with \bn{কিন্তু}, and give a reason for either with \bn{কেননা}.}

The first three-clause sentence in the track: a position, an objection to it, and a reason for the objection, built from \bn{কিন্তু}, \bn{একমত} and \bn{কেননা} over the negators and joiners of the two chapters before.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kintu]{\bn{কিন্তু} (kintu) — but}

\label{lesson:BN-C18-kintu}



\begin{quote}
The chapter before this joined things and offered a choice between them. Neither joiner can disagree with anything.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two joiners of the last chapter — \emph{ār}, \emph{bā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{কিন্তু}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{ভালো}, \bn{কিন্তু} \bn{আমার} \bn{চা} \bn{নেই}} — \emph{āmi bhālo, kintu āmār chā nei} — \textbf{I am well, but I have no tea.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আর}} puts two things on the same side. \textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} puts the second one against the first. It stands at the head of the clause it turns, after a comma in writing and after a small drop of the voice in speech.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} is Sanskrit \emph{kim-tu}, and both halves are recoverable. \emph{Kim} is \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} — the same ancient word standing behind \textbf{\bn{কি}}, which chapter three taught. \emph{Tu} is an old particle meaning \textquotedblleft{}however\textquotedblright{}. So \emph{but} in Bengali is literally \emph{what-however}, a shrug frozen into a conjunction.

Look at the middle of the written word: \textbf{\bn{ন্ত}} is \textbf{\bn{ন}} and \textbf{\bn{ত}} fused by the mark chapter two taught for deleting the inherent vowel. Two letters, one shape, and no new letter to learn.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmi bhālo, kintu āmār chā nei}
  \item the same two clauses with the other joiner — \emph{āmi bhālo ār āmār chā nei}
  \item and hear what changed — the second one no longer argues
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two Sanskrit pieces inside \textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}}? (\emph{\textbf{Kim}}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{\textbf{tu}}, \textquotedblleft{}however\textquotedblright{}.) Which word taught in chapter three is built on the first of them? (\textbf{\bn{কি}}.) And what does \textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} do that \textbf{\bn{আর}} cannot? (\textbf{Turn the second clause against the first}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ekmôt]{\bn{একমত} (ekmôt) — of one mind}

\label{lesson:BN-C18-ekmot}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আচ্ছা}} has been in this book since chapter one and it says \emph{I see}. It does not say \emph{I agree}, and nothing else here does either.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the word that turns a clause against the one before it — \emph{kintu}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{একমত}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{একমত}} — \emph{āmi ekmôt} — \textbf{I agree.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{একমত} \bn{নই}} — \emph{āmi ekmôt nôi} — \textbf{I do not agree.}
\end{quote}

The word is two words: \textbf{\bn{এক}}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}, which chapter twelve counted, and \textbf{\bn{মত}}, \textquotedblleft{}opinion\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Of one mind.} English builds the same picture out of Latin when it says \emph{unanimous} — \emph{ūnus animus}, one spirit.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: agreeing needs no verb, and disagreeing needs no new word}]
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{একমত}} has no verb in it, like \textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{ভালো}} before it — so it is denied the same way, with \textbf{\bn{নই}}. The whole of agreement and disagreement in Bengali is now two words the reader already owns arranged in two orders.

Put \textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} in front and you have the shape every conversation turns on: \textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{একমত}, \bn{কিন্তু} …} — \emph{I agree, but …}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmi ekmôt}
  \item \emph{āmi ekmôt nôi}
  \item the polite half-agreement — \emph{āmi ekmôt, kintu …}
  \item the one-word answers it can replace — \emph{hyã … nā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \textbf{\bn{একমত}}? (\emph{\textbf{Ek}}, one, and \emph{\textbf{môt}}, opinion.) Which negator denies it, and why that one? (\textbf{\bn{নই}} — the sentence has no verb to put \textbf{\bn{না}} after.) And which English word is built the same way out of Latin? (\textbf{Unanimous}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kenonā]{\bn{কেননা} (kenonā) — because}

\label{lesson:BN-C18-kenona}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons ago you could contradict somebody, and one lesson ago you could agree with them. Neither lets you say \textbf{why}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two items before this one — \emph{kintu}, \emph{ekmôt}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{কেননা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{একমত} \bn{নই}, \bn{কেননা} \bn{আমার} \bn{চা} \bn{নেই}} — \emph{āmi ekmôt nôi, kenonā āmār chā nei} — \textbf{I do not agree, because I have no tea.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{কেননা}} stands at the head of the reason, the way \textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} stands at the head of the objection. The order is fixed: the claim first, the reason after it.

\begin{cousinweb}
Pull \textbf{\bn{কেননা}} apart and the negator of chapter twenty-seven falls out of it: \textbf{\bn{কেন}} (\textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\bn{না}} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}). Bengali's word for \emph{because} is a rhetorical question worn smooth — \emph{why not?} — which is the same move English made in \emph{forasmuch as} and \emph{inasmuch as} before those went out of use.

Bengali writes another word here in everyday speech, \emph{kāraṇ}, from Sanskrit \emph{kāraṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}cause\textquotedblright{}. It is the commoner of the two and it needs a letter this book has not taught, so it is named in romanization and left for a script lesson. \textbf{\bn{কেননা}} costs no new letters at all — every piece of it is already yours.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmi ekmôt nôi, kenonā āmār chā nei}
  \item the two halves the word is made of — \emph{kænô … nā}
  \item an objection and then a reason — \emph{kintu … kenonā …}
  \item \emph{āmi jāni nā, kenonā āmi bhābi nā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words is \textbf{\bn{কেননা}} built from? (\textbf{\bn{কেন}}, why, and \textbf{\bn{না}}, not.) Which comes first, the claim or the reason? (\textbf{The claim} — the reason follows it.) And which word does the same job at the head of an objection? (\textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kintu · ekmôt · kenonā]{Agreeing, differing, and saying why}

\label{lesson:BN-R18-agree-and-differ}



\begin{quote}
Three items landed in this chapter, and between them they cover objecting, agreeing and explaining. Name all three.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āmi ekmôt} — then deny it, \emph{āmi ekmôt nôi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three-clause sentence — \emph{āmi ekmôt, kintu āmār chā nei, kenonā āmār dudh-o nei}
  \item \emph{Recall:} eight lessons back, the joiner that offers a choice — \emph{bā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} eleven lessons back, the negator of a verbless sentence — \emph{nôy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of this chapter's three words heads an objection, and which heads a reason? (\textbf{\bn{কিন্তু}} the objection; \textbf{\bn{কেননা}} the reason.) What is inside \textbf{\bn{কেননা}} that chapter twenty-seven taught? (\textbf{\bn{না}}.) And what would make the whole three-clause sentence a question? (\textbf{A rising voice at the end}, and nothing else.)
\end{tcolorbox}
